Build a Project Schedule for Critical Path and Schedule Risk Analysis.

Source: R/schedule.R
project_schedule.Rd

Assembles and validates a resource-loaded project schedule: activities, precedence links, duration uncertainty, resources with capacities and cost rates, resource assignments, and a register of discrete risk events. The result is the input to cpm() (deterministic critical path method) and sra() (Monte Carlo schedule risk analysis).

Usage

project_schedule(
  activities,
  links = NULL,
  duration_dists = NULL,
  resources = NULL,
  productivity_dists = NULL,
  assignments = NULL,
  risks = NULL,
  cor_mat = NULL,
  start_date = NULL,
  time_unit = "periods"
)

Arguments

activities

A data frame with one row per activity and columns id (required, unique), name (optional label, defaults to id), duration (non-negative baseline duration; may be NA for activities whose duration comes from a distribution or work assignments) and fixed_cost (optional non-resource cost, default 0).

links

A data frame of precedence links with columns source and target (activity ids), and optional type ("FS", "SS", "FF" or "SF", case-insensitive, default "FS") and lag (default 0). NULL for a schedule without links.

duration_dists

Optional named list of duration distributions, named by activity id.

resources

Optional data frame with columns id (required), capacity (positive units available, NA = unconstrained, default NA) and rate (non-negative cost per unit per time unit, default 0).

productivity_dists

Optional named list of productivity multiplier distributions, named by resource id. A draw of 0.8 makes that resource's work-driven activities take 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 times longer.

assignments

Optional data frame with columns activity, resource, units (positive units used per time unit while the activity runs) and optional work (positive total work; NA for an assignment that does not drive duration).

risks

Optional list of risk events; see Details.

cor_mat

Optional correlation matrix among the activities in duration_dists, in the order of names(duration_dists) or with matching dimnames. Must be positive definite. Induced by a Gaussian copula, as in mcs().

start_date

Optional project start Date (or a string coercible by as.Date()) used to label plot axes. Time is otherwise measured in abstract time_units from zero; calendars are not modelled.

time_unit

Character label for the time unit, such as "days" or "weeks". Used for labels only.

Value

An S3 object of class "pra_schedule": a list holding the validated and normalized inputs together with the topological order and adjacency matrix of the activity network. Objects of this class have print.pra_schedule(), summary.pra_schedule() and plot.pra_schedule() methods.

Details

Durations. Every activity needs exactly one duration source:

  • a fixed duration in activities;

  • an entry in duration_dists (its duration, if also given, is used as the deterministic baseline; otherwise the baseline is the mode of a triangular or PERT distribution, or the mean of a normal or uniform one);

  • work assignments (work in assignments), in which case the activity is resource-driven: its duration is the longest of work / (units * productivity) across its work assignments, with productivity 1 in the deterministic baseline. A resource-driven activity cannot also have a duration distribution; uncertainty enters through productivity_dists.

Links. Precedence links use the precedence diagramming method: FS (finish-to-start), SS (start-to-start), FF (finish-to-finish) and SF (start-to-finish), each with a lag in time units, which may be negative (a lead). Links must form a directed acyclic graph; a cycle is an error that names the activities on it.

Resources. A resource with a finite capacity is capacity-limited and is respected when scheduling with level = TRUE in cpm() or sra(); a capacity of NA means unconstrained. rate is cost per unit of resource per time unit, so an assignment costs units * rate * duration. No single assignment may need more units than its resource's capacity.

Risks. Each risk is a list with id, prob (probability of occurring in an iteration), activities (ids it affects), impact (a distribution of time added to each affected activity's duration when the risk occurs) and optionally cost_impact (a distribution of cost added when it occurs, shared equally among the affected activities for time-phasing).

Distributions. Distribution specifications use the same format as mcs(): a list with a type of "normal" (mean, sd), "triangular" (a = min, b = mode, c = max), "uniform" (min, max) or "pert" (a, b, c, the Beta-PERT distribution). Sampled durations are truncated at zero. Productivity multipliers must use a bounded type (triangular, uniform or PERT) with a positive minimum.

References

Damnjanovic, Ivan, and Kenneth Reinschmidt. Data analytics for engineering and construction project risk management. Cham, Switzerland: Springer, 2020.

Kolisch, Rainer. Serial and parallel resource-constrained project scheduling methods revisited: Theory and computation. European Journal of Operational Research 90.2 (1996): 320-333.

Examples

activities <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  duration = c(3, 5, 4, 2)
)
links <- data.frame(
  source = c("A", "A", "B", "C"),
  target = c("B", "C", "D", "D"),
  type = c("FS", "SS", "FS", "FF"),
  lag = c(0, 1, 0, 1)
)
duration_dists <- list(
  B = list(type = "triangular", a = 4, b = 5, c = 9),
  C = list(type = "pert", a = 3, b = 4, c = 7)
)
resources <- data.frame(id = "crew", capacity = 1, rate = 1000)
assignments <- data.frame(
  activity = c("B", "C"), resource = "crew", units = 1
)
risks <- list(
  list(
    id = "Late permit", prob = 0.3, activities = "A",
    impact = list(type = "uniform", min = 1, max = 3)
  )
)
proj <- project_schedule(activities, links,
  duration_dists = duration_dists, resources = resources,
  assignments = assignments, risks = risks, time_unit = "days"
)
proj
#> Project Schedule
#> Activities: 4   Links: 4   Resources: 1   Risks: 1 
#> Time unit: days
#> 
#>  id duration       driver predecessors
#>   A        3        fixed             
#>   B        5 distribution            A
#>   C        4 distribution        ASS+1
#>   D        2        fixed     B, CFF+1
